sources.text: Models - Meta Model API Skip to content Models Table of contents Meta ships six model lines. Muse Wonder , Muse Spark , Muse Image , Muse Voice Transcribe , and Segment Anything Model (SAM) are hosted on Meta Model API; Muse Glimmer is open-weight and runs on your own hardware. Pick one by what you're building, then read its section for versions and where to use them. Models at a glance Use case Model Input Output API endpoints Agentic work, coding, and reasoning Muse Wonder , Muse Spark Text, image, video, audio, and PDF Text Responses , Chat Completions , Messages Image generation and editing Muse Image Text and image Image Responses , Image generation Speech to text Muse Voice Transcribe Audio Text (transcription) Transcribe Image and video segmentation Segment Anything Model Text prompt, image, and video Text (geometry) Responses , Media segmentation Self-hosted inference; supervised fine-tuning Muse Glimmer Text and image Text None ( self-host ) Availability by country Model availability can vary by country. See the Geographic Use Policy for country-specific restrictions. Muse Wonder Muse Wonder is Meta's most capable model, built for complex software engineering and long-horizon agentic work. It makes and verifies changes across many files in real repositories, and it plans, delegates to sub-agents, calls tools in parallel, and recovers from errors across many steps, following detailed instructions closely. Take on hard coding tasks, build personal and professional agents, and drive a desktop with computer use . Muse Wonder also handles chat completion , image understanding , video and audio understanding , tool calling , structured output , and search grounding . Muse Wonder takes text, image, video, audio, and PDF input, returns text, has a 1,048,576-token context window, and supports reasoning effort levels from "minimal" to "max" . Preview Muse Wonder is in preview. For more about the model, see the Muse Wonder model page and the Muse Wonder model card (opens in new tab) . Muse Wonder availability Muse Wonder comes in two variants. Muse Wonder is on Model API and in Muse Code . Muse Wonder Full, the higher-capability variant, is available only in Muse Code with a subscription, so setting reasoning effort to "max" on Muse Wonder doesn't select it. Variant Model API (pay-as-you-go) Muse Code Muse Wonder ( muse-wonder-1.0 ) Available (Standard mode only) Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Wonder Full Not available Power Usage and Maximum Usage With a subscription, Muse Wonder is available on every plan and Muse Wonder Full on the Power Usage and Maximum Usage plans, each in Standard mode and Contributor mode . In Standard mode, your content — the prompts, code, files, and context you send, plus the model responses you get back — is not used to train Meta models. Muse Code subscribers can also use Contributor mode, which is on by default: it gives you more usage in exchange for letting Meta use your content to train future Meta models, and you can turn it off at any time in your settings. For Muse Wonder, Contributor mode isn't available on pay-as-you-go. See Pricing and rate limits for rates. Muse Spark Muse Spark is Meta's model for agentic and coding work — multi-step tool loops, software engineering assistants, and long-context reasoning. Use it for chat completion , image understanding , video and audio understanding , tool calling , structured output , and search grounding . Muse Spark comes in three versions. All take text, image, video, audio, and PDF input, return text, and have a 1,048,576-token context window. They differ by capability: Muse Spark 1.3 ( muse-spark-1.3 ): the latest version, tuned for agentic workflows (multi-step tool, browser, and long-horizon tasks) with improved coding over 1.2. Supports all reasoning effort levels, including the "max" level for extended reasoning (not available with muse-spark-1.3-contributor ). Recommended for new work. Muse Spark 1.2 ( muse-spark-1.2 ): the previous version. Muse Spark 1.1 ( muse-spark-1.1 ): the original version. Audio understanding in Muse Spark 1.3 is currently not fully supported, and response quality for requests including audio content may be degraded. For audio, use Muse Spark 1.2, or Muse Voice Transcribe for dedicated speech-to-text. muse-spark-1.3 is the default model in the code examples throughout these docs. Muse Spark availability Every Muse Spark version is available on pay-as-you-go. All versions except Muse Spark 1.1 are also available in Muse Code , on pay-as-you-go and with any subscription. Version Model API (pay-as-you-go) Muse Code Muse Spark 1.3 ( muse-spark-1.3 ) Standard mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor ( muse-spark-1.3-contributor ) Contributor mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.2 ( muse-spark-1.2 ) Standard mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.2 Contributor ( muse-spark-1.2-contributor ) Contributor mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.1 ( muse-spark-1.1 ) Standard mode Not available In Standard mode , your content is not used to train Meta models. In Contributor mode , your content may be used to train future Meta models, in exchange for a lower price. On pay-as-you-go, switch between the two by choosing the model ID: for example, muse-spark-1.3 for Standard mode or muse-spark-1.3-contributor for Contributor mode. Muse Spark 1.1 is available in Standard mode only. See Pricing and rate limits for rates. Choose Muse Wonder or Muse Spark Muse Wonder and Muse Spark take the same requests on the same endpoints, so moving a workload between them is a model ID change. Choose by workload: Muse Wonder : long-running, complex tasks where capability matters more than cost per token, such as multi-file coding changes, multi-hour agent runs, and sub-agent orchestration. Muse Spark : high-volume, latency-sensitive, or cost-sensitive work, such as sub-agent tasks, classification, and tight tool loops. On Model API, Muse Spark also offers a discounted Contributor mode . Muse Image Muse Image is Meta's image generation model line. Send a text prompt (and optional reference images) and get an image back, or send an image with an instruction to edit it. One model handles both generation and editing. It's agentic, so it can search the web for visual references and current facts and run code to build layouts before it renders. Model ID Input Output muse-image-1.0 Text, image Image Reach Muse Image two ways: the Responses API for conversational, multi-turn editing, or the single-shot /v1/images/generations and /v1/images/edits endpoints for one-off calls. See the Image generation guide to get started. Muse Voice Transcribe Muse Voice Transcribe is Meta's speech-to-text model on Meta Model API. Use it to transcribe live audio streams or supported audio files. Model ID Input Output muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 Audio Text transcript Muse Voice Transcribe is built for real-time speech products: voice agents, meeting and call intelligence, live transcription, dictation, captioning, and high-volume transcription. It supports streaming speaker diarization, native endpointing and voice activity detection, contextual and keyword biasing, 25 evaluated languages with code-switching, and turn-level timestamps. It returns transcript text. It does not synthesize speech or provide a speech-to-speech conversation API. It does not provide word-level timestamps, sound event detection, or emotion detection. Reach Muse Voice Transcribe two ways: the realtime WebSocket endpoint ( wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime ) for live audio, or the file endpoint ( POST /v1/asr/transcribe ) for a recording you already have. Start with the Muse Voice Transcribe guide . See Pricing and rate limits for audio pricing. Segment Anything Model SAM 3.1 is Meta's segmentation model on Meta Model API. Give it a short noun phrase such as "yellow school bus" with an image or video, and it returns every match as a box and a pixel-accurate mask. One model handles both stills and clips, and in video it follows each object across frames. Model ID Input Output sam-3.1 Text prompt, image, video Boxes and masks Reach SAM 3.1 over the Responses API ( POST /v1/responses ), and upload clips through the Files API when you segment them more than once. See the Media segmentation guide to get started. Muse Glimmer Muse Glimmer is Meta's open-weight multimodal model, distilled from Muse Spark and built to run on your own hardware. Unlike Muse Wonder, Muse Spark, Muse Image, Muse Voice Transcribe, and SAM, you don't call it over Model API — you download the weights and serve it through a runtime such as vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, or ExecuTorch. Muse Glimmer lives in the Open-weight models section, covering how to get, prompt, deploy, and customize the model: Muse Glimmer overview : variants, architecture, license, and launch partners. Get the model : download the weights and verify your setup. Run inference : pick a runtime and serve it locally. Fine-tune : adapt it to your domain with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), using LoRA, QLoRA, or full-parameter training. List models via the API Query the catalog programmatically when you need to check what's enabled for your team. This returns the API-hosted models; self-hosted Muse Glimmer isn't included. python import os ​ from openai import OpenAI ​ client = OpenAI ( base_url = "https://api.meta.ai/v1" , api_key = os . environ [ "MODEL_API_KEY" ] , ) ​ response = client . models . list ( ) ​ print ( response . model_dump_json ( indent = 2 ) ) python import json import os ​ import requests ​ response = requests . get ( "https://api.meta.ai/v1/models" , headers = { "Authorization" : f"Bearer {os.environ['MODEL_API_KEY']}" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) print ( json . dumps ( response . json ( ) , indent = 2 ) ) shell curl -X GET "https://api.meta.ai/v1/models" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY" The response returns models sorted newest-first by creation time, with the model ID as a stable tiebreaker. Each object includes a created field — the Unix timestamp in seconds for when the model was added to the registry. GET /v1/models/{model} returns the same created value for a single model. sources.text: Pricing and rate limits - Meta Model API Skip to content Pricing and rate limits Table of contents Use our models with pay-as-you-go billing on Meta Model API and in Muse Code , or in Muse Code with a monthly subscription . This page covers pay-as-you-go: Model API bills text models per token, image generation per image, Muse Voice Transcribe by the hour of audio processed, and Segment Anything Model (SAM) per image or video frame segmented, with no minimums or upfront commitment. Pricing modes Some models can be used in two modes. Standard mode uses standard pricing. Contributor mode offers discounted pricing or more usage in exchange for permission to use your content — the prompts, code, files, and context you send, plus the model responses you get back — to train future Meta models. Standard mode In Standard mode, you pay standard prices and your content is not used to train Meta models. Every model on this page is available in Standard mode. Contributor mode On Model API, Contributor mode runs the same models at heavily discounted token prices, in exchange for permission to use your content to train future Meta models. It lowers the barrier to entry for prototyping, testing integrations, and scaling experiments where it's acceptable for Meta to use your content to train future Meta models. On Model API, use Contributor mode with Muse Spark 1.3 or 1.2 by calling its Contributor-mode variant: muse-spark-1.3-contributor or muse-spark-1.2-contributor . Contributor mode isn't available for Muse Wonder on Model API. In Muse Code , subscriptions default to Contributor mode, and you can turn it on or off in settings; see Contributor mode in Muse Code . Model pricing Muse Wonder Model: muse-wonder-1.0 . Usage Standard mode (per 1M tokens) Contributor mode (per 1M tokens) Cached input $0.20 Not available Input $4.00 Not available Output $20.00 Not available Muse Spark Models: muse-spark-1.3 , muse-spark-1.2 , and muse-spark-1.1 in Standard mode; muse-spark-1.3-contributor and muse-spark-1.2-contributor in Contributor mode. Muse Spark 1.1 is Standard mode only. Usage Standard mode (per 1M tokens) Contributor mode (per 1M tokens) Cached input $0.15 $0.002 Input $1.25 $0.10 Output $4.25 $0.20 Token pricing notes These apply to the token-priced models above, Muse Wonder and Muse Spark. Cached input costs less : When part of your prompt matches a cached prefix , you pay the cached-input rate for those tokens. Check cached_tokens in the response to see how many were served from cache. No long-context premium : you pay the same rate whether your context window is mostly empty or almost full. Web search grounding : $2.50 per 1,000 search queries , in addition to the request's token cost. This applies to the web_search tool on text models such as Muse Wonder and Muse Spark . Muse Image search is included Muse Image 's built-in web and image search is part of its per-image price and isn't charged separately. See Muse Image pricing . Muse Image Usage Price Generated image $0.01 per image Muse Image is billed at a flat rate per generated image. The price is the same regardless of prompt length, reasoning_strength , or the tools the model uses during generation, including its built-in web and image search, which isn't charged separately. A request that returns n images is billed for n images. You're billed only for images the model successfully generates and returns: images that fail to generate, or that are removed by safety filtering before they're returned, aren't counted. Image responses still include a usage object with token counts for reference, but image generation tokens are not included in token-based pricing for other models. See the Image generation guide for the response shape. Muse Voice Transcribe Muse Voice Transcribe is billed by audio processed, metered in whole seconds. Usage Price Audio processed $0.18 per hour Streaming and non-streaming transcription are priced the same. Zero data retention (ZDR) is priced at parity with Standard mode. Contributor mode isn't available for Muse Voice Transcribe. Audio time is billed as a separate line item from token usage, rounded down to whole seconds; other endpoints aren't billed for audio time. Segment Anything Model 3.1 SAM 3.1 segmentation is billed per image and per video frame, not per token. The same prices apply to streaming and non-streaming requests. Usage Price Image segmentation $2.50 per 1,000 images Video segmentation $0.20 per 1,000 frames Rate limits Rate limits apply per team, not per API key : requests, tokens, and streams from every key in a team count toward the same limits. Each model below has its own limits, so traffic to one model doesn't use up another's. Model Requests per minute (RPM) Tokens per minute (TPM) Other limits muse-wonder-1.0 3,000 4,000,000 muse-spark-1.3 3,000 4,000,000 muse-spark-1.2 3,000 4,000,000 muse-spark-1.3-contributor 150 3,000,000 muse-spark-1.2-contributor 150 3,000,000 muse-spark-1.1 3,000 4,000,000 sam-3.1 3,000 None muse-image-1.0 150 None muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 None None 256 concurrent streams; 16,000 streams per hour SAM 3.1 is billed per image or frame and Muse Image is priced per image , so neither has a TPM limit. Muse Voice Transcribe is billed by audio processed , so it's limited by streams rather than requests or tokens. Concurrent streams caps how many transcription sessions you hold open at once; streams per hour caps how many you start. Realtime and file transcription share the same budget. Token usage counts only your input and output tokens. Meta injects a small amount of steering context into every prompt (a system prompt and related scaffolding); those injected tokens are not billed and are excluded from the token counts reported in your usage and by the token-counting endpoints . Background responses Creating background responses ( background: true ) is limited to 600 submissions per minute, per team , in addition to the limits above. The cap applies only to starting new background responses: over it, new submissions return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, and responses already running continue unaffected. Handle rate limits When you exceed a limit, the API rejects the request. Requests succeed again once usage drops below the limit. Retry on 429 responses Retry strategy: Use exponential backoff with jitter. Start with a short delay such as 500 ms, double it after each consecutive rate-limit response, and add random jitter to avoid thundering-herd effects across concurrent clients. If the response includes a Retry-After header, wait at least that long. Read rate-limit headers Every successful token-based response includes headers that report your current limit and remaining quota: Header Description x-ratelimit-limit-tokens Total token budget for the current window. x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens Tokens remaining before you hit the limit. x-ratelimit-limit-requests Total request budget for the current window. x-ratelimit-remaining-requests Requests remaining before you hit the limit. Read these headers and slow down before you hit a rate limit instead of reacting after one. Handle Muse Voice Transcribe rejections A realtime stream rejected for exceeding a stream limit closes with 1013 . A rejected file-transcription request returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests . Transcription responses don't include the x-ratelimit-* headers. How it works When you send a request, the model works through the problem internally first. That reasoning stays private and does not appear in the response body. Reasoning tokens count toward your output-token budget ( max_tokens on Chat Completions, max_output_tokens on the Responses API) and toward billed output tokens. Set reasoning_effort to choose depth: Value Behavior "none" Disables reasoning. Not supported by Muse Wonder or Muse Spark : returns HTTP 400 . "minimal" Shortest reasoning pass. "low" Light reasoning. "medium" Moderate depth. "high" Deep reasoning. "xhigh" Deeper reasoning. "max" Extended reasoning beyond "xhigh" . Supported by muse-wonder-1.0 and muse-spark-1.3 ; not available with muse-spark-1.3-contributor . Higher effort means more reasoning — and more reasoning tokens, latency, and cost. "none" disables reasoning entirely, which Muse Wonder and Muse Spark do not support. Max reasoning The "max" level on Muse Wonder and Muse Spark 1.3 goes beyond "xhigh" : the model spends more time reasoning before responding, using more reasoning tokens at the same per-token price as other effort levels. It isn't available with muse-spark-1.3-contributor , the Contributor-mode variant of Muse Spark 1.3. In Muse Code, Muse Wonder Full also supports max ; see Set reasoning

Token usage Reasoning tokens count toward both your output-token limit and billed completion tokens: Output-token limit : max_tokens (Chat Completions) and max_output_tokens (Responses API) cap reasoning tokens plus visible output tokens combined. If the model spends most of the budget on reasoning, the visible response may be truncated. Set the limit high enough to accommodate both. Billing : Reasoning tokens are billed at the same rate as visible output tokens. The usage breakdown reports them separately as completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens (Chat Completions) or output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens (Responses API). Higher reasoning_effort produces more reasoning tokens, which means longer latency and higher cost. Use the lowest level that gives you acceptable results. At "max" , reasoning tokens make up a larger share of output_tokens than at lower efforts, so set the output-token limit generously. When to reach for reasoning Higher reasoning effort helps with multi-step problem solving: proofs and calculations, complex code generation, architecture trade-off analysis, and task planning and sequencing. sources.text: Subscriptions - Meta Model API Skip to content Subscriptions Table of contents With a Muse Code subscription, you pay a flat monthly rate for usage of Muse Code , instead of paying per token. Subscription benefits and availability may vary by region. Available benefits will be shown to you during onboarding before you subscribe. About subscriptions To sign up for a Muse Code subscription, you will need a Meta Account. Using your Meta Account, you can create an associated Meta Model API account and sign up for a subscription. The subscription applies to the Muse Code API key that is automatically connected in the Muse Code CLI onboarding process. This credential is for use with Muse Code only. Any additional API keys you create under your Meta Model API account will be billed through pay-as-you-go . You must be 18 or the age of majority in your country to subscribe. Your subscription is subject to the Meta Subscription Terms of Service (opens in new tab) , and your use of Muse Code and the Meta Model API is governed by the Meta Model API Terms of Service and the Meta Model API Acceptable Use Policy . How Meta uses your content — the prompts, code, files, and context you send, plus the model responses you get back — depends on whether Contributor mode is on in your settings, and is described in the Meta Model API Terms of Service . There are 4 subscription plans available for Muse Code: Everyday Usage Access to the Muse model family Send 10-50 prompts every 5 hours, including image and video uploads Use voice mode Get access to web search High Usage Everything from the Everyday Usage plan 5x more usage than the Everyday Usage plan More multimodal inputs Power Usage Everything from the High Usage plan Access to the most powerful Muse models 20x more usage than the Everyday Usage plan Early access to new features Higher file uploads Maximum Usage Everything from the Power Usage plan 80x more usage than the Everyday Usage plan Contributor mode Muse Code subscriptions default to Contributor mode. In Contributor mode, you get more usage from your plan in exchange for letting Meta use your content to train future Meta models. Contributor mode is a setting in Muse Code, and you can turn it off at any time, at which point your future content is not used to train Meta models (unless you turn it back on in your settings). Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are each available in either mode on the plans that include them. For the models each plan includes, see Muse Wonder availability . Choose pay-as-you-go or a subscription Muse Code supports 2 ways to pay for usage: Pay-as-you-go : billed per token consumed with your Meta Model API key. See billing and plans . Subscription : a flat monthly rate (see the plans above). It works only through the Muse Code CLI while signed in with your Meta Model API account. If you reach your plan's usage limit, you can upgrade to the next plan, or wait until your limit refreshes. If you are on the Maximum Usage plan, you must wait for your limit to refresh. Usage through any additional API keys you create is billed pay-as-you-go. Subscribe Sign in to Muse Code with your Meta Model API account on dev.meta.ai , then subscribe through Accounts Center: Go to Subscriptions in Accounts Center (opens in new tab) . Select Muse Code , then choose a plan and complete checkout. On success, you will see a confirmation screen with a link to your receipt and the option to Manage your subscription . Change or cancel your plan Manage your plan from Manage your subscription on the Subscriptions page in Accounts Center (opens in new tab) . From an interactive session, type /upgrade to open Accounts Center in your browser. Upgrade : A plan upgrade takes effect immediately. You will be charged a prorated amount for the rest of the current billing cycle. Downgrade : A plan downgrade takes effect at the start of your next billing cycle. You will keep your current plan's usage limit until the next billing cycle. Cancel : From Accounts Center, go to Manage your subscription and select Cancel subscription . Your subscription stays active until the end of the current billing cycle, then you lose access to all benefits. Cancel at least 24 hours before your next billing date to avoid future charges. What happens when your subscription ends A subscription ends one of 2 ways: you can cancel it (see Change or cancel your plan ), or Meta can revoke it. Revocation is different from cancellation. When your subscription is revoked, you lose access immediately instead of at the end of your billing cycle. Meta may revoke a subscription for various reasons, including: Payment failure : your payment method fails and you have no backup payment method on file. Policy violation : your account violates the Model API terms , Meta's Community Standards (opens in new tab) or Meta Subscription Terms of Service (opens in new tab) . Account deletion or deactivation : deleting your account cancels the subscription immediately. Deactivating your account keeps the subscription active for 30 days. If you don't reactivate within that window, Meta revokes it. Loss of eligibility : for example, your account no longer meets the age requirement, or you move to a restricted territory. To subscribe again after a revocation, your account must meet the eligibility requirements in About subscriptions . Billing cycle Your subscription renews automatically each month on the date you first subscribed. If that date doesn't exist in a given month (for example, the 31st in a 30-day month), you're charged on the last day of that month instead. Manage your payment method and view billing history from Accounts Center (opens in new tab) . No refunds for canceled subscriptions : if you cancel your subscription, you won't receive a credit or refund unless required by law. Next steps Set up sign-in and pay-as-you-go billing in authentication and billing . Start your first session in the overview . sources.text: Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents Skip to main content Loading demo Play Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Play Show captions for Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Show captions Mute Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. Mute Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. playback position 0:00 of 0:00 00:00 / 00:00 A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish. Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code , and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers. Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse , and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse. Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier. When we introduced Muse Spark , we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products. Frontier Capabilities Model Highlights The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding. The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite. For more details about our evaluations, see our report . The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding. Domain Expertise Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products. Active Memory One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory : carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand. Active Focus Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects. Frontier Coding Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process. Kitchen Game Wellness Support Insurance Claim Kitchen Game Loading demo Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs. Capabilities That Generalize Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture. To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”). Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training. Muse Wonder designs and orders custom swag based on real photos taken from a personal Instagram profile. Muse Wonder prepares a custom wedding seating chart based on a list of complex matching requirements. Safety at the Frontier Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information. As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework . Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon. We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. sources.text: Muse Wonder Model Card This card describes the Muse Wonder models, the evaluations we ran, and the limits of that testing. 1. The models Name Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full Model Provider Meta Platforms, Inc. or Meta Platforms Ireland Limited Website dev.meta.ai Date of Release October 12, 2026 Modalities Input: text, image, video, audio Output: text Languages The model was trained on multilingual training data, with substantial representation across worldwide languages. Context Length 1M tokens at inference Contact https://dev.meta.ai/support 2. Intended uses The Muse Wonder models are intended for commercial and research use, with particular strengths in personal and professional agentic tasks. Th ... ... Overall Methodology ● Models and configurations. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full results are generated with max reasoning effort. We compare with GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 at max reasoning effort. For controlled internal coding comparisons, every model uses the same benchmark-specific harness. External coding results retain the harness or agent product used by the reporting vendor or model provider, and that source is identified below. ● Evaluation and score selection. We preserve each benchmark’s tasks, inputs, grading, and primary metric as closely as possible. Where a comparable third-party or provider-reported result exists, we use it; otherwise we use the highest of our internally validated run, self-reported score, or official leaderboard score. Benchmark names link to official leaderboards where available. Model refusals receive zero credit and remain in the denominator rather than being dropped. Material departures from the official setup are noted below. ● Competitor-model results. Internally generated competitor runs use common settings where practical but remain best-effort: prompts, tools, and runtime may not be optimally tuned for proprietary models. Per-benchmark details Personal and Professional Agents ● Personal Superintelligence Index (PSI). PSI is an internal composite of seven personal and knowledge-work evaluations: Agents’ Last Exam, AutomationBench-AA, FocusBench, JobBench, GDP.pdf, VBT, and DRACO. ● Harvey LAB-AA. Harvey LAB-AA is Artificial Analysis’s version of Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, in which agents produce legal work products from matter documents and an Artificial Analysis judge panel checks each deliverable against task-specific criteria. We report version 1.1, which adds hallucination checks. The result sou ... MemoryBench. MemoryBench is an internal benchmark that tests how accurately a model can recall critical information across long, complex multi-turn conversations of 64K to 100K tokens that span several individual facts, with distractor conversations and injected turns that conflict with or later update the target details. An LLM judge scores each answer against weighted, question-specific rubric criteria. ● Verifiable Browsing Task (VBT). VBT is an internal agentic web-browsing evaluation in which models answer list-style information-seeking questions, written as realistic user requests, using browser search, open, and find tools. ● Deep Research Accuracy, Completeness, and Objectivity (DRACO). DRACO, from Perplexity, is a deep-research benchmark of 100 complex, multi-domain questions. ... DeepSWE v1.1. DeepSWE is a long-horizon software-engineering benchmark with 113 tasks across 91 repositories and five languages. Handwritten functional and regression tests grade each task, and the primary metric is pass@1. The scorecard uses Datacurve’s third-party results for Muse Wonder, Muse Wonder Full, and Claude Opus 5.5, and OpenAI’s provider-reported result for GPT-6 Astra. For Claude Fable 5.1, we use the result reported in Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 system card. ● SWE-Marathon. SWE-Marathon is an ultra-long-horizon software-engineering benchmark of substantial projects graded by executing project tests. The primary metric is pass@1. Abundant AI is the result source for all models. Its leaderboard results for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 use Codex and Claude Code, respectively, so this row is not a controlled common-harness comparison. Muse Wonder Full was reported with xhigh reasoning effort. ● ProgramBench. ProgramBench evaluates whether an agent can reconstruct a complete program in a clean-room environment. Each submission is compiled and graded by a hidden behavioral test suite, with internet access disabled after setup. All compared models use mini-swe-agent. The primary metric is the percentage of rollouts passing at least 95% of tests. General ● AA Intelligence Index v4.3. AA Intelligence Index v4.3 is Artificial Analysis’s composite index. It combines evaluations Artificial Analysis runs independently, including GDPval-AA, AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf, Terminal-Bench 4.0, SciCode, AA-LCR, AA-Omniscience, CritPt, and Humanity’s Last Exam, into a single score. The result source is Artificial Analysis, and the primary metric is the index score. ... 6. Considerations and Limitations Muse Wonder is a technology that carries known and unknown risks. Testing conducted to date has not covered, and could not cover, all scenarios. Limitations 1. The model may produce inaccurate, biased, or objectionable responses to user prompts. 2. While optimized for agentic tasks, the model may still make errors in multi-step reasoning, particularly in novel scenarios not well represented in training data. 3. Visual and spatial reasoning, especially 3D tasks, remains a known limitation. Validate performance for applications that depend on precise spatial understanding. 4. The model has not been evaluated on all languages contained in the pre-training data. Performance may degrade on languages outside the strongly supported set. 5. Performance can vary with quantization, serving configuration, prompts, tools, and the agent harness. 6. The model is not intended to be used by individuals under the age of 18. Deployers are responsible for ensuring that any risks associated with such use by individuals ... under the age of 18 have been fully assessed and appropriately mitigated, and that such use complies with all applicable laws. Muse Wonder's use is subject to the restrictions and conditions in the applicable terms of use, including the Meta Model API Terms of Service (https://dev.meta.ai/legal/terms-of-service), Meta Model Acceptable Use Policy (https://dev.meta.ai/legal/acceptable-use-policy), and Muse Supplemental Terms of Service (https://muse.ai/terms). Responsible Use Developers should conduct their own evaluation of whether the model is appropriate for their deployment, with assessments tailored to their specific applications and proposed languages. We recommend implementing additional guardrails (such as human-in-the-loop confirmation for irreversible actions) when deploying the model in agentic contexts where it can take real-world actions. Feature-specific pricing  Prompt caching  Prompt caching reduces costs and latency by reusing previously processed portions of your prompt across API calls. Instead of reprocessing the same large system prompt, document, or conversation history on every request, the API reads from cache at a fraction of the standard input price. There are two ways to enable prompt caching: Automatic caching: Add a single cache_control field at the top level of your request. The system automatically manages cache breakpoints as conversations grow. This is the recommended starting point for most use cases. Explicit cache breakpoints: Place cache_control directly on individual content blocks for fine-grained control over exactly what gets cached. Prompt caching uses the following pricing multipliers relative to base input token rates: Cache operation Multiplier Duration 5-minute cache write 1.25x base input price Cache valid for 5 minutes 1-hour cache write 2x base input price Cache valid for 1 hour Cache read (hit) 0.1x base input price (0.025x on Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1; 0.05x on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5) Same duration as the preceding write Cache write tokens are charged when content is first stored. Cache read tokens are charged when a subsequent request retrieves the cached content. A cache hit costs 10% of the standard input price, which means caching pays off after one cache read for the 5-minute duration (1.25x write), or after two cache reads for the 1-hour duration (2x write). On Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, a cache hit costs 2.5% of the standard input price ($0.25 USD per million tokens). On Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, a cache hit costs 5% of the standard input price ($0.20 USD per million tokens on Claude Opus 5.5, $0.10 USD on Claude Sonnet 5.5). These multipliers stack with other pricing modifiers, including the Batch API discount and data residency. For implementation details, supported models, and code examples, see Prompt caching . Data residency pricing  For Claude 4.6 and later models, specifying US-only inference through the inference_geo parameter incurs a 1.1x multiplier on all token pricing categories, including input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads. On Claude Haiku 5.5, the multiplier also applies to the higher prices for prompts over 100,000 tokens (see Long context pricing ). Global routing (the default) uses standard pricing. This applies to the Claude API (first-party) and Claude Platform on AWS. On Claude in Microsoft Foundry, the same 1.1x multiplier applies to deployments that use the US Data Zone Standard deployment type (see Inference geography ). Partner-operated platforms (Bedrock and Google Cloud) have independent regional pricing. See Bedrock and Google Cloud for details. Earlier models do not support the inference_geo parameter and always use standard pricing; requests that include the parameter on these models return a 400 error. For more information, see Data residency . Fast mode pricing  Fast mode , in research preview, provides significantly faster output for Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Opus 4.8 at premium pricing. Fast mode pricing applies across the full context window, including requests over 200k input tokens. Fast mode is available on the Claude API (first-party) only; it is not available on Claude Platform on AWS or partner-operated cloud platforms. (A 900k-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9k-token request.) Prompt caching and batch processing discounts apply at standard rates across the full context window. Claude Haiku 5.5 is priced by prompt length: a request whose prompt is over 100,000 tokens pays higher prices. A request's prompt length counts all of its input tokens, including cache reads and cache writes. Each request is priced on its own: a request over the threshold pays the higher prices even when part of its prompt is a cache hit, and earlier requests keep the prices they were billed at. Model pricing and Batch processing list both sets of prices. Tool use pricing  Tool use requests are priced based on: The total number of input tokens sent to the model (including in the tools parameter) The number of output tokens generated For server-side tools, additional usage-based pricing (for example, web search charges per search performed) Client-side tools are priced the same as any other Claude API request, although server-side tools can incur additional charges based on their specific usage. The additional tokens from tool use come from: The tools parameter in API requests (tool names, descriptions, and schemas) tool_use content blocks in API requests and responses tool_result content blocks in API requests When you use tools , the API also automatically includes a special system prompt for the model that enables tool use. Code execution tool  Code execution is free when used with web search or web fetch. When web_search_20260209 (or later) or web_fetch_20260209 (or later) is included in your API request, there are no additional charges for code execution tool calls beyond the standard input and output token costs. When used without these tools, code execution is billed by execution time, tracked separately from token usage: Execution time has a minimum of 5 minutes Each organization receives 1,550 free hours of usage per month Additional usage beyond 1,550 hours is billed at $0.05 USD per hour, per container If files are included in the request, execution time is billed even if the tool is not called, because files are preloaded onto the container Code execution usage is tracked in the response: { "usage" : { "input_tokens" : 105 , "output_tokens" : 239 , "server_tool_use" : { "code_execution_requests" : 1 } } }  Text editor tool  The text editor tool uses the same pricing structure as other tools used with Claude. It follows the standard input and output token pricing based on the Claude model you're using. In addition to the base tokens, the following additional input tokens are needed for the text editor tool: Tool Additional input tokens text_editor_20250728 (Claude 4.7 and later models and Claude Mythos Preview) 974 tokens text_editor_20250728 (Claude 4.6 and earlier models) 745 tokens See tool use pricing for complete pricing details. Web search tool  Web search usage is charged in addition to token usage: { "usage" : { "input_tokens" : 105 , "output_tokens" : 6039 , "cache_read_input_tokens" : 7123 , "cache_creation_input_tokens" : 7345 , "server_tool_use" : { "web_search_requests" : 1 } } }  Web search is available on the Claude API for $10 per 1,000 searches , plus standard token costs for search-generated content. Web search results retrieved throughout a conversation are counted as input tokens, in search iterations executed during a single turn and in subsequent conversation turns. Each web search counts as one use, regardless of the number of results returned. If an error occurs during web search, the web search will not be billed. Web fetch tool  Web fetch usage has no additional charges beyond standard token costs: { "usage" : { "input_tokens" : 25039 , "output_tokens" : 931 , "cache_read_input_tokens" : 0 , "cache_creation_input_tokens" : 0 , "server_tool_use" : { "web_fetch_requests" : 1 } } }  The web fetch tool is available on the Claude API at no additional cost . You only pay standard token costs for the fetched content that becomes part of your conversation context. To protect against inadvertently fetching large content that would consume excessive tokens, use the max_content_tokens parameter to set appropriate limits based on your use case and budget considerations. Example token usage for typical content: Average web page (10 kB): ~2,500 tokens Large documentation page (100 kB): ~25,000 tokens Research paper PDF (500 kB): ~125,000 tokens Computer use tool  Computer use follows the standard tool use pricing . When using the computer use tool: Toolset definition overhead: Declaring computer_toolset_20260801 with its default members adds about 4,500 input tokens to a request (about 4,590 on Claude Sonnet 5 and about 4,520 on the other supported models), which covers the member tool definitions and the tool use system prompt. Disabling zoom with configs removes about 410 of those tokens. The exact count for a request is reported in the response usage , and you can estimate it in advance with the token counting endpoint . Earlier tool versions: The following figures apply to the computer_20251124 and computer_20250124 tool versions, not to computer_toolset_20260801 : System prompt overhead: 466–499 tokens added to the system prompt Tool definition: about 735 input tokens per tool definition (measured with computer_20250124 ) Additional token consumption: Screenshot and zoom images returned in tool results, billed as image input (see Vision pricing ) Tool execution results returned to Claude  If you're also using bash or text editor tools alongside computer use, those tools have their own token costs as documented in their respective pages. Browser use tool  Browser use follows the standard tool use pricing . When using the browser use tool: Toolset definition overhead: Declaring browser_toolset_20260801 with its default members adds about 6,600 input tokens to a request (about 6,670 on Claude Sonnet 5 and about 6,610 on the other supported models), which covers the member tool definitions and the tool use system prompt. Enabling all four optional members adds about 880 tokens, and disabling members with configs reduces the count. The exact count for a request is reported in the response usage , and you can estimate it in advance with the token counting endpoint . Additional token consumption: Screenshot and zoom images returned in tool results, billed as image input (see Vision pricing ) Text tool results returned to Claude, such as accessibility trees, page text, and console or network entries  If you also use the computer use tool, bash tool, text editor tool, or your own tools alongside browser use, those tools have their own token costs as documented on their respective pages. Claude Managed Agents pricing  Claude Managed Agents is billed on two dimensions: tokens and session runtime. Tokens  All tokens consumed by a Claude Managed Agents session are billed at the rates shown in Model pricing . Prompt caching multipliers apply identically. Web search triggered inside a session incurs the standard $10 per 1,000 searches. On Claude Platform on AWS , session token and runtime charges convert to Claude Consumption Units at the standard rate. Fast mode premium pricing applies when an agent's model.speed is set to "fast" . The data residency multiplier also applies: when an agent's model.inference_geo is pinned to "us" , tokens consumed by sessions running that agent are billed at 1.1x the standard rates, the same multiplier that applies to US-only inference on the Messages API. The following Messages API modifiers do not apply to Claude Managed Agents sessions: Modifier Why it doesn't apply Batch API discount Sessions are stateful and interactive. There is no batch mode. Cloud platform pricing Not available on partner-operated cloud platforms. Session runtime  SKU Rate Metering Session runtime $0.08 per session-hour running status duration Runtime is measured to the millisecond and accrues only while the session's status is running . Time spent idle (waiting for your next message or a tool confirmation), rescheduling , or terminated does not count toward runtime.  Session runtime replaces the code execution container-hour billing model when using Claude Managed Agents. You are not separately billed for container hours on top of session runtime. Worked example  A one-hour coding session using Claude Opus 5 that consumes 50,000 input tokens and 15,000 output tokens: Line item Calculation Cost Input tokens 50,000 × $5 / 1,000,000 $0.25 Output tokens 15,000 × $25 / 1,000,000 $0.375 Session runtime 1.0 hour × $0.08 $0.08 Total $0.705 If prompt caching is active and 40,000 of the input tokens are cache reads: Line item Calculation Cost Uncached input tokens 10,000 × $5 / 1,000,000 $0.05 Cache read tokens 40,000 × $5 × 0.1 / 1,000,000 $0.02 Output tokens 15,000 × $25 / 1,000,000 $0.375 Session runtime 1.0 hour × $0.08 $0.08 Total $0.525 Additional pricing considerations  Cost optimization strategies  When building agents with Claude: Use appropriate models: Choose Haiku for simple tasks, Sonnet for most production workloads, and Opus for the most complex reasoning Implement prompt caching: Reduce costs for repeated context Batch operations: Use the Batch API for non-time-sensitive tasks Monitor usage patterns: Track token consumption to identify optimization opportunities  For high-volume agent applications, contact the enterprise sales team for custom pricing arrangements. Rate limits  Rate limits vary by usage tier and affect how many requests you can make: Start tier: Entry-level limits for getting started Build tier: Increased limits for growing applications Scale tier: Highest standard limits for production workloads For detailed rate limit information, see Rate limits . For limits beyond the Scale tier or custom pricing arrangements, contact the sales team . Volume discounts  Volume discounts may be available for high-volume users. These are negotiated on a case-by-case basis. Standard usage tiers use the pricing shown in Model pricing Enterprise customers can contact sales for custom pricing Academic and research discounts may be available Enterprise pricing  For enterprise customers with specific needs: Custom rate limits Volume discounts Dedicated support Custom terms Contact the sales team at sales@anthropic.com or through the Claude Console to discuss enterprise pricing options. Billing and payment  Billing is based on actual monthly usage All payments are in USD Credit card and invoicing options available Usage tracking available in the Claude Console Frequently asked questions  How is token usage calculated?  Tokens are pieces of text that models process. How many tokens the same text produces depends on the model's tokenizer, the language, and the type of content. Claude 4.7 and later models and Claude Mythos Preview use a newer tokenizer that produces approximately 30 percent more tokens for the same text than earlier models. To see how many tokens a request uses on a specific model, count it with token counting and that model's ID. Are there free tiers or trials?  New users receive a small amount of free credits to test the API. Contact sales for information about extended trials for enterprise evaluation. How do discounts stack?  Batch API and prompt caching discounts can be combined. For example, using both features together provides significant cost savings compared to standard API calls. See prompt caching pricing for how the multipliers interact. What payment methods are accepted?  Major credit cards are accepted for standard accounts. Enterprise customers can arrange invoicing and other payment methods. For additional questions about pricing, contact support@anthropic.com . Was this page helpful?   Ask Docs 

summary.text: 표준 API의 백만 토큰당 입력은 4달러, 출력은 20달러로 Claude Opus 5.5와 같습니다. GPT-6 Astra와 Claude Fable 5.1의 기본 입력은 10달러, 출력은 50달러여서 Wonder보다 높습니다. Spark 1.3은 입력 1.25달러, 출력 4.25달러로 Wonder보다 낮습니다. 실제 업무 비용이나 속도를 독립 측정한 결과는 아닙니다.

explanation.title: 모델 개요와 이전 계열에서의 변화
explanation.lead: Wonder 계열은 Spark의 단순한 이름 변경이 아니라 새 기반 모델 계열로 발표됐습니다.

blocks.title: Spark에서 Wonder로
blocks.text: Meta는 Spark에서 구축한 학습, 확장 기반 위에 더 강한 모델을 만들고 긴 작업, 기억과 집중을 학습했다고 설명합니다. 공식 모델 목록은 Spark와 Wonder를 별도 모델로 제공합니다. 이전 계열 대비 정확한 개선율을 계산할 공통 Spark 평가 행은 이번 카드에 없으므로 경쟁 표에 임의 수치를 채우지 않았습니다.

blocks.title: Active Memory와 Active Focus
blocks.text: Active Memory는 대화에서 중요한 정보를 다시 찾아 유지하는 능력, Active Focus는 긴 작업 중 새 정보에 맞추어 접근을 조정하고 진행을 이어가는 능력이라는 Meta의 설명입니다. 학습 방향과 제공자의 기능 설명이며 외부 영구 데이터베이스나 무오류 실행을 보장하지 않습니다. Wonder는 API 모델, Muse Code는 이를 사용하는 개발 제품이고 Full은 그 제품의 일부 구독에서 제공하는 별도 상위 모델입니다.

explanation.title: 성능 비교 해석
explanation.lead: 동일 이름의 평가라도 측정 주체와 작업 환경이 다르면 점수 차이를 그대로 모델의 우열로 해석하기 어렵습니다.

blocks.title: 코드 평가의 측정 주체와 도구
blocks.text: DeepSWE 1.1은 91개 저장소, 5개 언어의 113개 작업에서 기능, 회귀 테스트를 평가하는 pass@1, 즉 첫 시도의 성공 비율입니다. 카드에서 Wonder 계열과 Opus는 Datacurve 측정, Astra는 OpenAI 자체 보고, Fable은 Anthropic 시스템 카드에서 가져옵니다. SWE-Marathon은 Abundant AI 결과를 인용하며 경쟁 모델에 Codex, Claude Code가 사용됐으므로 공통 Harness 비교가 아닙니다. Harness는 모델에 도구와 실행, 평가 환경을 연결하는 틀입니다. 이 행의 Full은 xhigh로 다른 max 결과와 설정도 다릅니다.

blocks.title: 프로그램 재구성과 기억 평가의 의미
blocks.text: ProgramBench는 준비 후 네트워크를 끄고 mini-swe-agent로 프로그램을 재구성합니다. 수치는 숨겨진 테스트의 95% 이상을 통과한 rollout의 비율이며 모든 테스트의 통과율을 뜻하지 않습니다. MemoryBench는 Meta 내부 평가로 64,000~100,000 토큰 길이의 대화에 방해 정보와 갱신된 사실을 섞고 LLM이 가중 기준으로 판정합니다. 백만 토큰 문맥 전체나 영구 기억을 검증한 점수가 아닙니다.

blocks.title: 컴퓨터 조작과 종합 지표
blocks.text: OSWorld V2.1은 108개 Ubuntu 데스크톱 작업을 평가합니다. 평균 부분 점수와 완전 완료율은 별개이며 Opus는 제공자 보고 부분 점수만 있어 완료율을 미공개로 남겼습니다. Terminal-Bench와 AA Intelligence Index는 카드가 인용한 Artificial Analysis 결과입니다. AA 지수는 여러 평가를 묶은 점수이고 정답률이 아닙니다. 원 실행 기록 전체를 독립 대조한 것은 아닙니다. 카드 자체도 가능한 타사, 제공자 결과를 활용하고 그 외에는 내부, 자체 보고, 공식 순위 중 높은 검증 결과를 선택한다고 설명합니다.

explanation.title: 장점
explanation.lead: 평가 결과와 제공 조건에서 확인되는 상대적 강점을 정리했습니다.

blocks.title: 일부 장기 코드, 기억 평가의 강점
blocks.text: 코드 과제 첫 시도 성공률인 DeepSWE에서 Wonder는 78.8%로 Astra 74.1%, Opus 74.2%, Fable 67.4%보다 높습니다. 장기 프로젝트 성공률인 SWE-Marathon도 Wonder 53.1%로 Astra 42.5%, Opus 46.3%, Fable 45.6%보다 높습니다. MemoryBench 가중 점수는 Wonder 85.6으로 Full 85.5와 경쟁군의 79.0~81.5보다 높습니다. 장기 코드 작업과 대화 정보 유지에 강점이 나타난 근거지만, 각 행의 측정 조건과 Meta 내부 LLM 판정 한계를 함께 봐야 합니다.

blocks.title: API 제공과 상대적인 가격 위치
blocks.text: Full과 달리 공개 API가 있고 텍스트 외 이미지, 영상, 음성, PDF를 입력할 수 있습니다. 백만 토큰당 표준 입력 4달러, 출력 20달러는 Astra와 Fable의 기본 입력 10달러, 출력 50달러보다 낮으며 장문 할증도 없습니다. 다만 Opus와 토큰 단가는 같고 Spark보다 높으므로 최저가 모델이라 부를 수는 없습니다.

explanation.title: 단점과 한계
explanation.lead: 반대 결과와 접근 제약도 모델 선택의 근거에 포함했습니다.

blocks.title: 코드, 컴퓨터 조작, 종합 지표의 약점
blocks.text: ProgramBench의 기준 충족 실행 비율은 Wonder 50.0%로 Opus 70.5%, Fable 55.5%, Astra 52.5%보다 낮습니다. Terminal-Bench 정확도도 Wonder 52.0%로 Astra 59.1%, Opus 59.6%보다 낮고 Fable 52.0%와 같습니다. OSWorld 부분 점수는 Wonder 72.6으로 경쟁군의 75.8~81.8보다 낮습니다. AA 종합 지수는 Wonder 52점으로 Full 56점, Opus 58점, Fable과 Astra의 53점보다 낮아 일부 강점만으로 전반적 우위라 말할 수 없습니다.

blocks.title: 제공 상태와 확인되지 않은 성능
blocks.text: API는 preview이며 지역별 제공 조건과 개별 계정 접근은 별도입니다. 최대 출력 토큰을 이번 공식 문서 검토에서 확인하지 못했습니다. 모델 카드도 새로운 상황의 여러 단계 추론 오류,3D 공간 이해와 언어별 평가 공백을 명시합니다. 한국어 성능, 응답 속도, 실제 개발 업무의 비용 절감은 이 표로 증명되지 않습니다.

explanation.title: 가격과 제공 조건
explanation.lead: 표준 토큰 단가와 구독 플랜은 서로 다른 결제 단위입니다.

blocks.title: Wonder와 경쟁 API의 가격 차이
blocks.text: Wonder의 백만 토큰당 표준 입력 요금은 4달러, 출력 요금은 20달러로 Opus 5.5와 같습니다. Astra와 Fable의 기본 입력 10달러, 출력 50달러보다 낮지만 이전 Spark 1.3의 입력 1.25달러, 출력 4.25달러보다는 높습니다. 이는 해당 요금 항목의 비교이며 특정 작업이 같은 토큰량이나 같은 정확도로 끝난다는 뜻은 아닙니다. Astra는 입력이 272K 토큰을 초과하면 전체 요청의 입력과 캐시 요금을 2배, 출력 요금을 1.5배로 과금합니다. Meta에는 장문 할증이 없고 Fable과 Opus의 기본 1M 토큰 문맥도 장문 할증이 없습니다.

blocks.title: 추론과 도구 과금
blocks.text: Wonder의 내부 추론 토큰도 출력 요금에 포함됩니다. Meta 웹 검색은 검색 질의 1,000개당 2.50달러를 별도 청구합니다. 캐시 읽기 단가는 입력 전체에 적용되는 할인율이 아니며 캐시에서 실제 재사용한 부분에만 적용됩니다. 가격표의 출력 단가만으로 실제 답변 길이, 추론량, 검색량과 실행 시간을 알 수 없습니다.

blocks.title: Full 구독과 데이터 사용
blocks.text: Full은 Muse Code의 Power 플랜에서 월 50달러, Maximum 플랜에서 월 200달러에 제공합니다. Everyday 플랜 대비 Power는 20배, Maximum은 80배의 사용량을 제공하며, 이는 모델 성능 배수나 고정 토큰 수, 무제한 사용량을 뜻하지 않습니다. 구독은 Contributor mode가 기본으로 켜져 있어 더 많은 사용량을 받는 대신 프롬프트, 코드, 파일, 문맥, 응답을 향후 Meta 모델 학습에 사용할 수 있습니다. 끄면 이후 콘텐츠를 이 용도로 사용하지 않으며 과거 콘텐츠의 소급 삭제를 보장하는 설명은 아닙니다. Standard mode 콘텐츠는 학습에 사용하지 않는다고 명시합니다. 구독 전용 자격과 추가 PAYG 키의 청구는 분리되며 추가 키가 Full API 접근을 열지는 않습니다.

result.title: 일부 코드, 기억 평가와 API 가격에 강점이 있으나 전반적 우위는 아닙니다

points.label: 성능의 위치
points.text: Wonder는 DeepSWE, SWE-Marathon, MemoryBench에 강점이 있고 ProgramBench, Terminal-Bench, OSWorld, AA에서 뒤지는 항목이 있습니다.

points.label: 선택 조건
points.text: 멀티모달 입력과 공개 API, 해당 표준 요금이 필요한 경우의 후보입니다. Opus와 같은 토큰 단가이므로 표의 유리한 행과 불리한 행을 함께 비교할 근거가 있습니다.

caveats.text: 이 자료는 공식 소개, 사양, 가격과 카드의 평가 원문을 비교한 분석입니다. 모델 실행이나 독립 평가를 수행하지 않았으며 전체 벤치마크, 안전성 부록, 지역 접근, 실제 청구를 모두 확인한 것은 아닙니다.
가중치 공개, 매개변수 수, 로컬 실행 메모리와 별도 배포 라이선스는 이번 범위에서 확인하지 않았습니다. 다른 Meta 모델의 조건을 그대로 적용하지 않습니다.

Pick one by what you're building, then read its section for versions and where to use them. Models at a glance Use case Model Input Output API endpoints Agentic work, coding, and reasoning Muse Wonder , Muse Spark Text, image, video, audio, and PDF Text Responses , Chat Completions , Messages Image generation and editing Muse Image Text and image Image Responses , Image generation Speech to text Muse Voice Transcribe Audio Text (transcription) Transcribe Image and video segmentation Segment Anything Model Text prompt, image, and video Text (geometry) Responses , Media segmentation Self-hosted inference; supervised fine-tuning Muse Glimmer Text and image Text None ( self-host ) Availability by country Model availability can vary by country. See the Geographic Use Policy for country-specific restrictions. Muse Wonder Muse Wonder is Meta's most capable model, built for complex software engineering and long-horizon agentic work. It makes and verifies changes across many files in real repositories, and it plans, delegates to sub-agents, calls tools in parallel, and recovers from errors across many steps, following detailed instructions closely. Take on hard coding tasks, build personal and professional agents, and drive a desktop with computer use . Muse Wonder also handles chat completion , image understanding , video and audio understanding , tool calling , structured output , and search grounding . Muse Wonder takes text, image, video, audio, and PDF input, returns text, has a 1,048,576-token context window, and supports reasoning effort levels from "minimal" to "max" . Preview Muse Wonder is in preview. For more about the model, see the Muse Wonder model page and the Muse Wonder model card (opens in new tab) . Muse Wonder availability Muse Wonder comes in two variants. Muse Wonder is on Model API and in Muse Code . Muse Wonder Full, the higher-capability variant, is available only in Muse Code with a subscription, so setting reasoning effort to "max" on Muse Wonder doesn't select it. Variant Model API (pay-as-you-go) Muse Code Muse Wonder ( muse-wonder-1.0 ) Available (Standard mode only) Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Wonder Full Not available Power Usage and Maximum Usage With a subscription, Muse Wonder is available on every plan and Muse Wonder Full on the Power Usage and Maximum Usage plans, each in Standard mode and Contributor mode . In Standard mode, your content — the prompts, code, files, and context you send, plus the model responses you get back — is not used to train Meta models. Muse Code subscribers can also use Contributor mode, which is on by default: it gives you more usage in exchange for letting Meta use your content to train future Meta models, and you can turn it off at any time in your settings. For Muse Wonder, Contributor mode isn't available on pay-as-you-go. See Pricing and rate limits for rates. Muse Spark Muse Spark is Meta's model for agentic and coding work — multi-step tool loops, software engineering assistants, and long-context reasoning. Use it for chat completion , image understanding , video and audio understanding , tool calling , structured output , and search grounding . Muse Spark comes in three versions. All take text, image, video, audio, and PDF input, return text, and have a 1,048,576-token context window. They differ by capability: Muse Spark 1.3 ( muse-spark-1.3 ): the latest version, tuned for agentic workflows (multi-step tool, browser, and long-horizon tasks) with improved coding over 1.2. Supports all reasoning effort levels, including the "max" level for extended reasoning (not available with muse-spark-1.3-contributor ). Recommended for new work. Muse Spark 1.2 ( muse-spark-1.2 ): the previous version. Muse Spark 1.1 ( muse-spark-1.1 ): the original version. Audio understanding in Muse Spark 1.3 is currently not fully supported, and response quality for requests including audio content may be degraded. For audio, use Muse Spark 1.2, or Muse Voice Transcribe for dedicated speech-to-text. muse-spark-1.3 is the default model in the code examples throughout these docs. Muse Spark availability Every Muse Spark version is available on pay-as-you-go. All versions except Muse Spark 1.1 are also available in Muse Code , on pay-as-you-go and with any subscription. Version Model API (pay-as-you-go) Muse Code Muse Spark 1.3 ( muse-spark-1.3 ) Standard mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor ( muse-spark-1.3-contributor ) Contributor mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.2 ( muse-spark-1.2 ) Standard mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.2 Contributor ( muse-spark-1.2-contributor ) Contributor mode Pay-as-you-go and every plan Muse Spark 1.1 ( muse-spark-1.1 ) Standard mode Not available In Standard mode , your content is not used to train Meta models. In Contributor mode , your content may be used to train future Meta models, in exchange for a lower price. On pay-as-you-go, switch between the two by choosing the model ID: for example, muse-spark-1.3 for Standard mode or muse-spark-1.3-contributor for Contributor mode. Muse Spark 1.1 is available in Standard mode only. See Pricing and rate limits for rates. Choose Muse Wonder or Muse Spark Muse Wonder and Muse Spark take the same requests on the same endpoints, so moving a workload between them is a model ID change. Choose by workload: Muse Wonder : long-running, complex tasks where capability matters more than cost per token, such as multi-file coding changes, multi-hour agent runs, and sub-agent orchestration. Muse Spark : high-volume, latency-sensitive, or cost-sensitive work, such as sub-agent tasks, classification, and tight tool loops. On Model API, Muse Spark also offers a discounted Contributor mode . Muse Image Muse Image is Meta's image generation model line. Send a text prompt (and optional reference images) and get an image back, or send an image with an instruction to edit it. One model handles both generation and editing. It's agentic, so it can search the web for visual references and current facts and run code to build layouts before it renders. Model ID Input Output muse-image-1.0 Text, image Image Reach Muse Image two ways: the Responses API for conversational, multi-turn editing, or the single-shot /v1/images/generations and /v1/images/edits endpoints for one-off calls. See the Image generation guide to get started. Muse Voice Transcribe Muse Voice Transcribe is Meta's speech-to-text model on Meta Model API. Use it to transcribe live audio streams or supported audio files. Model ID Input Output muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 Audio Text transcript Muse Voice Transcribe is built for real-time speech products: voice agents, meeting and call intelligence, live transcription, dictation, captioning, and high-volume transcription. It supports streaming speaker diarization, native endpointing and voice activity detection, contextual and keyword biasing, 25 evaluated languages with code-switching, and turn-level timestamps. It returns transcript text. It does not synthesize speech or provide a speech-to-speech conversation API. It does not provide word-level timestamps, sound event detection, or emotion detection. Reach Muse Voice Transcribe two ways: the realtime WebSocket endpoint ( wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime ) for live audio, or the file endpoint ( POST /v1/asr/transcribe ) for a recording you already have. Start with the Muse Voice Transcribe guide . See Pricing and rate limits for audio pricing. Segment Anything Model SAM 3.1 is Meta's segmentation model on Meta Model API. Give it a short noun phrase such as "yellow school bus" with an image or video, and it returns every match as a box and a pixel-accurate mask. One model handles both stills and clips, and in video it follows each object across frames. Model ID Input Output sam-3.1 Text prompt, image, video Boxes and masks Reach SAM 3.1 over the Responses API ( POST /v1/responses ), and upload clips through the Files API when you segment them more than once. See the Media segmentation guide to get started. Muse Glimmer Muse Glimmer is Meta's open-weight multimodal model, distilled from Muse Spark and built to run on your own hardware. Unlike Muse Wonder, Muse Spark, Muse Image, Muse Voice Transcribe, and SAM, you don't call it over Model API — you download the weights and serve it through a runtime such as vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, or ExecuTorch. Muse Glimmer lives in the Open-weight models section, covering how to get, prompt, deploy, and customize the model: Muse Glimmer overview : variants, architecture, license, and launch partners. Get the model : download the weights and verify your setup. Run inference : pick a runtime and serve it locally. Fine-tune : adapt it to your domain with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), using LoRA, QLoRA, or full-parameter training. List models via the API Query the catalog programmatically when you need to check what's enabled for your team. This returns the API-hosted models; self-hosted Muse Glimmer isn't included. python import os ​ from openai import OpenAI ​ client = OpenAI ( base_url = "https://api.meta.ai/v1" , api_key = os . environ [ "MODEL_API_KEY" ] , ) ​ response = client . models . list ( ) ​ print ( response . model_dump_json ( indent = 2 ) ) python import json import os ​ import requests ​ response = requests . get ( "https://api.meta.ai/v1/models" , headers = { "Authorization" : f"Bearer {os.environ['MODEL_API_KEY']}" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) print ( json . dumps ( response . json ( ) , indent = 2 ) ) shell curl -X GET "https://api.meta.ai/v1/models" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY" The response returns models sorted newest-first by creation time, with the model ID as a stable tiebreaker. Each object includes a created field — the Unix timestamp in seconds for when the model was added to the registry. GET /v1/models/{model} returns the same created value for a single model. sources.text: Pricing and rate limits - Meta Model API Skip to content Pricing and rate limits Table of contents Use our models with pay-as-you-go billing on Meta Model API and in Muse Code , or in Muse Code with a monthly subscription . This page covers pay-as-you-go: Model API bills text models per token, image generation per image, Muse Voice Transcribe by the hour of audio processed, and Segment Anything Model (SAM) per image or video frame segmented, with no minimums or upfront commitment. Pricing modes Some models can be used in two modes. Standard mode uses standard pricing. Contributor mode offers discounted pricing or more usage in exchange for permission to use your content — the prompts, code, files, and context you send, plus the model responses you get back — to train future Meta models. Standard mode In Standard mode, you pay standard prices and your content is not used to train Meta models. Every model on this page is available in Standard mode. Contributor mode On Model API, Contributor mode runs the same models at heavily discounted token prices, in exchange for permission to use your content to train future Meta models. It lowers the barrier to entry for prototyping, testing integrations, and scaling experiments where it's acceptable for Meta to use your content to train future Meta models. On Model API, use Contributor mode with Muse Spark 1.3 or 1.2 by calling its Contributor-mode variant: muse-spark-1.3-contributor or muse-spark-1.2-contributor . Contributor mode isn't available for Muse Wonder on Model API. In Muse Code , subscriptions default to Contributor mode, and you can turn it on or off in settings; see Contributor mode in Muse Code . Model pricing Muse Wonder Model: muse-wonder-1.0 . Usage Standard mode (per 1M tokens) Contributor mode (per 1M tokens) Cached input $0.20 Not available Input $4.00 Not available Output $20.00 Not available Muse Spark Models: muse-spark-1.3 , muse-spark-1.2 , and muse-spark-1.1 in Standard mode; muse-spark-1.3-contributor and muse-spark-1.2-contributor in Contributor mode. Muse Spark 1.1 is Standard mode only. Usage Standard mode (per 1M tokens) Contributor mode (per 1M tokens) Cached input $0.15 $0.002 Input $1.25 $0.10 Output $4.25 $0.20 Token pricing notes These apply to the token-priced models above, Muse Wonder and Muse Spark. Cached input costs less : When part of your prompt matches a cached prefix , you pay the cached-input rate for those tokens. Check cached_tokens in the response to see how many were served from cache. No long-context premium : you pay the same rate whether your context window is mostly empty or almost full. Web search grounding : $2.50 per 1,000 search queries , in addition to the request's token cost. This applies to the web_search tool on text models such as Muse Wonder and Muse Spark . Muse Image search is included Muse Image 's built-in web and image search is part of its per-image price and isn't charged separately. See Muse Image pricing . Muse Image Usage Price Generated image $0.01 per image Muse Image is billed at a flat rate per generated image. The price is the same regardless of prompt length, reasoning_strength , or the tools the model uses during generation, including its built-in web and image search, which isn't charged separately. A request that returns n images is billed for n images. You're billed only for images the model successfully generates and returns: images that fail to generate, or that are removed by safety filtering before they're returned, aren't counted. Image responses still include a usage object with token counts for reference, but image generation tokens are not included in token-based pricing for other models. See the Image generation guide for the response shape. Muse Voice Transcribe Muse Voice Transcribe is billed by audio processed, metered in whole seconds. Usage Price Audio processed $0.18 per hour Streaming and non-streaming transcription are priced the same. Zero data retention (ZDR) is priced at parity with Standard mode. Contributor mode isn't available for Muse Voice Transcribe. Audio time is billed as a separate line item from token usage, rounded down to whole seconds; other endpoints aren't billed for audio time. Segment Anything Model 3.1 SAM 3.1 segmentation is billed per image and per video frame, not per token. The same prices apply to streaming and non-streaming requests. Usage Price Image segmentation $2.50 per 1,000 images Video segmentation $0.20 per 1,000 frames Rate limits Rate limits apply per team, not per API key : requests, tokens, and streams from every key in a team count toward the same limits. Each model below has its own limits, so traffic to one model doesn't use up another's. Model Requests per minute (RPM) Tokens per minute (TPM) Other limits muse-wonder-1.0 3,000 4,000,000 muse-spark-1.3 3,000 4,000,000 muse-spark-1.2 3,000 4,000,000 muse-spark-1.3-contributor 150 3,000,000 muse-spark-1.2-contributor 150 3,000,000 muse-spark-1.1 3,000 4,000,000 sam-3.1 3,000 None muse-image-1.0 150 None muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 None None 256 concurrent streams; 16,000 streams per hour SAM 3.1 is billed per image or frame and Muse Image is priced per image , so neither has a TPM limit. Muse Voice Transcribe is billed by audio processed , so it's limited by streams rather than requests or tokens. Concurrent streams caps how many transcription sessions you hold open at once; streams per hour caps how many you start. Realtime and file transcription share the same budget. Token usage counts only your input and output tokens. Meta injects a small amount of steering context into every prompt (a system prompt and related scaffolding); those injected tokens are not billed and are excluded from the token counts reported in your usage and by the token-counting endpoints . Background responses Creating background responses ( background: true ) is limited to 600 submissions per minute, per team , in addition to the limits above. The cap applies only to starting new background responses: over it, new submissions return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, and responses already running continue unaffected. Handle rate limits When you exceed a limit, the API rejects the request. Requests succeed again once usage drops below the limit. Retry on 429 responses Retry strategy: Use exponential backoff with jitter. Start with a short delay such as 500 ms, double it after each consecutive rate-limit response, and add random jitter to avoid thundering-herd effects across concurrent clients. If the response includes a Retry-After header, wait at least that long. Read rate-limit headers Every successful token-based response includes headers that report your current limit and remaining quota: Header Description x-ratelimit-limit-tokens Total token budget for the current window. x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens Tokens remaining before you hit the limit. x-ratelimit-limit-requests Total request budget for the current window. x-ratelimit-remaining-requests Requests remaining before you hit the limit. Read these headers and slow down before you hit a rate limit instead of reacting after one. Handle Muse Voice Transcribe rejections A realtime stream rejected for exceeding a stream limit closes with 1013 . A rejected file-transcription request returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests . Transcription responses don't include the x-ratelimit-* headers. How it works When you send a request, the model works through the problem internally first. That reasoning stays private and does not appear in the response body. Reasoning tokens count toward your output-token budget ( max_tokens on Chat Completions, max_output_tokens on the Responses API) and toward billed output tokens. Set reasoning_effort to choose depth: Value Behavior "none" Disables reasoning. Not supported by Muse Wonder or Muse Spark : returns HTTP 400 . "minimal" Shortest reasoning pass. "low" Light reasoning. "medium" Moderate depth. "high" Deep reasoning. "xhigh" Deeper reasoning. "max" Extended reasoning beyond "xhigh" . Supported by muse-wonder-1.0 and muse-spark-1.3 ; not available with muse-spark-1.3-contributor . Higher effort means more reasoning — and more reasoning tokens, latency, and cost. "none" disables reasoning entirely, which Muse Wonder and Muse Spark do not support. Max reasoning The "max" level on Muse Wonder and Muse Spark 1.3 goes beyond "xhigh" : the model spends more time reasoning before responding, using more reasoning tokens at the same per-token price as other effort levels.
